title: Cat and Mouse in Partnership
paragraphs: A certain cat had made friends with a mouse, and had told her so often how much love and friendship she felt for her that in the end the mouse agreed to live and keep house with her. “But we must lay in a supply for the winter, or we’ll go hungry,” said the cat. “And you, little mouse, can’t go poking about everywhere, or you’ll end up in a trap some day.” They took this good advice and bought a pot of fat, but they couldn’t decide where to put it. After thinking it over for a long time, the cat said, “I can’t think of a better place to keep it than the church, because nobody dares steal anything from there. We’ll tuck it under the altar and not touch it until we really need it.” So the pot was put away safely, but before long the cat was longing for it, and she said to the mouse, “I have something to tell you, little mouse. My cousin has had a baby boy and has asked me to be his godmother. He’s white with brown spots, and I’m to hold him over the font at the christening. Let me go out today, and you look after the house by yourself.” “Yes, yes,” answered the mouse, “by all means go. And if you get anything really good to eat, think of me. I’d love a drop of that sweet red christening wine myself.” None of it was true, though. The cat had no cousin and had not been asked to be anyone’s godmother. She went straight to the church, crept up to the pot of fat, started licking, and licked off the top layer. Then she strolled over the rooftops of the town, looked out for chances, stretched out in the sun, and licked her lips whenever she thought of the pot of fat. She did not come home until evening. “Well, there you are again,” said the mouse. “I’m sure you’ve had a lovely day.” “It all went well,” said the cat. “What did they name the child?” “Top-off!” said the cat, perfectly calm. “Top-off!” cried the mouse. “That’s a very strange and unusual name. Is it common in your family?” “What does it matter?” said the cat. “It’s no worse than Crumb-stealer, which is what your godchildren are called.”

Before long the cat was seized by another fit of longing. She said to the mouse, “You’ll have to do me a favor and run the house alone for another day. I’ve been asked to be godmother again, and since the child has a white ring around its neck, I can’t say no.” The good mouse agreed, but the cat sneaked along behind the town walls to the church and ate up half the pot of fat. “Nothing tastes as good as what you keep to yourself,” she said, and she was thoroughly pleased with her day’s work. When she got home, the mouse asked, “And what was this child christened?” “Half-done,” answered the cat. “Half-done! What are you saying? I’ve never heard that name in my life. I’ll bet you anything it isn’t in the calendar!”

The cat’s mouth soon began to water for more licking. “All good things come in threes,” she said. “I’ve been asked to be godmother again. The child is jet black, with only white paws, and not one other white hair on its whole body. That happens only once every few years. You’ll let me go, won’t you?” “Top-off! Half-done!” answered the mouse. “Such strange names. They make me think.” “That’s because you sit at home in your dark-gray fur coat and your long tail,” said the cat, “and fill your head with fancies. It comes of never going out in the daytime.” While the cat was away, the mouse cleaned the house and put it in order, but the greedy cat emptied the pot of fat completely. “Once everything is eaten up, a body gets some peace,” she told herself, and she came home only at nightfall, well fed and plump. The mouse asked at once what the third child had been named. “You won’t like it any better than the others,” said the cat. “He’s called All-gone.” “All-gone!” cried the mouse. “That is the most suspicious name of all! I’ve never seen it in print. All-gone. What can that mean?” She shook her head, curled up and went to sleep.

From then on nobody invited the cat to be a godmother. But when winter came and there was nothing left to find outside, the mouse remembered their store and said, “Come, cat, let’s go to our pot of fat that we put away for ourselves. We’ll enjoy that.” “Yes,” answered the cat, “you’ll enjoy it about as much as sticking that dainty tongue of yours out of the window.” They set off, and when they got there, the pot of fat was indeed still in its place, but it was empty. “Oh no,” said the mouse, “now I see what happened. Now it comes out! You’re a fine friend! You ate it all while you were off being godmother. First top-off, then half-done, then—” “Hold your tongue,” cried the cat, “or say one more word and I’ll eat you too.” “All-gone” was already on the poor mouse’s lips. She had barely said it when the cat sprang on her, seized her and swallowed her down. That, truly, is the way of the world.
